title: What we look for
desc: Twenty-one categories, the backwards sensitivity dial, your own terms and the allowlist that leaks by design.
learningGoal: After this lesson you can choose categories and a sensitivity level you are able to defend, and add a company term and an exception without opening a hole.

steps.title: The shield can be on and still find nothing
steps.bodyMd:
Van Dijk Groep is a sixty-person installation firm near Zwolle, and its shield is switched on — that was the previous chapter. On its own, that proves nothing. A shield asked the wrong questions reports itself as protecting you while every customer name sails straight past it.

This tab sets the questions. Open `Settings` → `Organisation` → `Privacy Shield` and pick **What we look for**. It settles three of them:

- which kinds of personal data the detector is asked about
- how sure it has to be before a finding counts
- which words of your own are always hidden, and which are deliberately left visible

All four policy tabs save together, with one button at the bottom right: **Save All Changes**. Until you press it, nothing you do here is in force.

steps.title: An unticked category is never even asked about
steps.bodyMd:
Under **Kinds of personal data** sit **21** checkboxes in two columns, with `All` and `None` buttons and a live count in the heading: `Kinds of personal data (7/21)`. Labels run from Person Names and Email Addresses to National ID numbers (BSN and equivalents).

Leave a box unticked and that kind of data is never put to the detector. The question is never asked, so the answer always comes back clean — and nothing in your reports hints at the gap.

Emptying the list is not a choice either. The **Overview** row `Kinds of data we look for` then warns in amber — "Protection is on, but nothing is ticked — so nothing will ever be found." — while the scanner reads an empty list as "never configured" and scans all 21 anyway. Two parts of the product disagreeing is not a policy: tick what you mean.

steps.title: The dial runs backwards
steps.bodyMd:
**How strict should we be?** offers three cards: `Low sensitivity`, `Balanced` (badged `Recommended`) and `High sensitivity`. Behind them is one number — how sure the detector must be before a finding counts — and it runs opposite to the names: Low sensitivity is **85%**, Balanced **70%**, High sensitivity **45%**. Lower number, more findings.

Balanced is not a split-the-difference compromise. It is the calibrated anchor: every per-category level is tuned and measured at that position, so it is the only setting whose behaviour has actually been tested.

`Advanced: set an exact percentage` reveals a slider from 10% to 100% in steps of 5, labelled "Find more (10%)" at one end and "Find less (100%)" at the other. Anything off-preset shows as `Custom · NN%` — a number you will have to justify.

steps.question: Van Dijk Groep's admin opens the advanced slider and sets 90%, reasoning that a higher number must be stricter. What actually happens?

choices.label: Almost nothing is hidden — the detector now has to be 90% sure, and most short messages never score that high.
Everything even slightly personal is hidden, and colleagues start complaining about false alarms.
choices.feedback: That is what a LOW number does. The slider is a confidence threshold, not a strictness score: 10% finds the most, 100% the least.

choices.label: Only the high-risk categories are still checked; names and company names are dropped.
choices.feedback: The threshold never changes which categories are asked — that is the list of categories. It only changes how sure the detector must be about each finding.

choices.label: Nothing changes, because the slider only takes effect once the Balanced card is deselected.
choices.feedback: Moving the slider off a preset value is the deselection — the card stops being highlighted and a `Custom · 90%` chip appears instead.

steps.explanation: The dial is inverted, which is exactly why the three named cards exist. At 85% or above the page pushes back itself, in amber: "At this setting almost nothing is hidden. Short messages usually score between 60% and 85%…". `Balanced` (70%) is the answer you can defend, because that is the level everything was measured at.

steps.title: Always hide these: your own words
steps.bodyMd:
Fold open **Your own words and exceptions**. The first panel, **Always hide these**, covers what the 21 categories cannot know about: project code names, contract-number formats, internal system names.

Type a name in `Give it a name`, press `Add`, then fill in `What to look for` and choose between `Exact text` and `Pattern (advanced)`; `Case sensitive` starts off. Van Dijk Groep adds one row: name `Inkoopcontractnummer`, pattern `VDG-INK-\d{6}`, type `Pattern (advanced)`.

Two things make this panel worth the effort. Your terms are hidden **on top of** whatever the detector finds. And Bee Flow matches them itself, character for character: no model weighs them up, so the sensitivity setting does not apply — a pattern either matches or it does not.

steps.title: Never hide these: exact, everywhere, forever
steps.bodyMd:
The amber panel below does the opposite, and it is the one control on this page that makes the shield leak on purpose. Values under **Never hide these** are left visible to the AI, every time.

Three properties to hold on to:

- **Exact.** Matching is on the normalised value — case, spaces and punctuation ignored — and never a substring. Allowing "Shell" does not allow "Shell Advies BV"; each variant needs its own entry.
- **Everywhere.** Your own entries apply in **every** category, not just company names.
- **Forever.** There is no expiry. An entry stands until somebody deletes it.

Above the chips sits **Always allow well-known companies**, on by default: a shipped list of 221 large companies, brands and public bodies. That list applies to the `Company names` category only; yours are not limited that way.

steps.question: To keep AI answers readable, the admin types "Van Dijk" into Never hide these. What did they just exempt?

choices.label: Every value that normalises to "vandijk" — in all 21 categories, including a customer or an employee named Van Dijk.
"Van Dijk" and anything containing it, such as "Van Dijk Groep" and "Van Dijk Installatie BV".
choices.feedback: Matching is exact on the normalised value, never a substring — that is deliberate, because substring matching would silently unredact a different company. "Van Dijk Groep" needs its own entry.

choices.label: Only the Company names category, since an allow term is an exception to organisation detection.
choices.feedback: That limit applies to the built-in well-known-companies list. A term you type yourself is honoured whichever detector flagged the value.

choices.label: Nothing yet — allow terms only take effect once Always allow well-known companies is switched off.
choices.feedback: The two sources are independent switches. Your own list works whether the built-in list is on or off.

steps.explanation: An allow term is a permanent, cross-category exemption on an exact value. Short and common words are the danger: a surname that doubles as a company name buys you readability in one chat and unredacted people everywhere else. Write the full, specific form — "Van Dijk Groep" — and add each variant you actually need.

steps.title: Four teams, four defensible sets
steps.instruction: The sixty people at Van Dijk Groep sit in four teams, and each works with different data. Match the team to the set of categories that has to be ticked before their work is protected.

pairs.left: Inkoop pastes supplier quotations into chat to compare prices, contract numbers and payment details.
pairs.right: IBAN Numbers, Bank Account Numbers, Tax numbers (VAT / BTW / RSIN)
pairs.note: Financial counterparty data. Company names belongs here too — but tick it and a redacted price comparison becomes unreadable, which is the exact itch that sends admins to Never hide these.

pairs.left: HR runs a nightly routine that summarises sick-leave and re-integration files.
pairs.right: National ID numbers (BSN and equivalents), Medical Conditions, Medications
pairs.note: Special-category data plus the BSN. Nobody is watching a routine at night, so the categories are the only protection in the room.

pairs.left: Support pastes a customer e-mail into chat to draft a friendly reply.
pairs.right: Person Names, Email Addresses, Phone Numbers
pairs.note: The everyday case, and the highest volume. If only these three are ticked you already cover most of what leaves a support desk.

pairs.left: IT pastes a server log into chat while debugging a broken connector.
pairs.right: IP Addresses, Passwords and access keys, Web addresses
pairs.note: Logs are personal data too: an IP address identifies a person, and a pasted log is the classic way an access key reaches a model.

steps.title: Read the save bar, not just the button
steps.bodyMd:
The server compiles your patterns when you save. If one will not compile, the rest of the shield is stored anyway — the save is partial, not refused. So the only place you learn your pattern is not running is the message beside **Save All Changes**:

- a green toast **"Saved successfully!"** — everything went in
- amber **"Saved, with notes — see the message below."**, and below it "Saved, but 1 custom term(s) were rejected and are not in force." The offending row turns red with "Not saved — " and the engine's own complaint.
- amber **"Saved. Note: …"** — a setting your plan does not cover was stored at the value it allows

One trap: reloading or closing the page warns you about unsaved changes; clicking to another screen inside the app does not — those edits are gone.

steps.title: Add one term and one exception — we will verify it
steps.instruction: Open the Privacy Shield, go to the tab What we look for and fold open Your own words and exceptions. Under Always hide these, add one term of your own — a contract-number pattern or an internal project name. Under Never hide these, add your organisation's full name, not the short one. Press Save All Changes and read the message beside the button: green means both rows are in force. You can delete either row again afterwards.

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.bodyMd:
- **Pick categories on purpose.** An unticked one is never asked about; the grid heading and the **Overview** row `Kinds of data we look for` both count what you chose, and zero means nothing will ever be found.
- **Defend the level, not the word.** Balanced (70%) is the measured setting; a higher percentage finds less, not more, whatever "strict" suggests.
- **Use both exception lists with your eyes open.** Always hide these widens the net with text and patterns Bee Flow matches itself; Never hide these is exact, applies in every category and never expires — so write the full name, never the short one.

Next chapter: what actually happens to a message once something is found, and what may still leave your organisation.

practiceTopic.title: Privacy Shield detection settings
practiceTopic.summary: How an organisation admin chooses categories, sensitivity and exception lists on the What we look for tab.
facts: The Kinds of personal data grid holds 21 checkboxes in two columns with All and None buttons and a live count in its heading, for example 'Kinds of personal data (7/21)'.
Sensitivity cards map to confidence thresholds that run backwards: Low sensitivity 85%, Balanced 70% (badged Recommended), High sensitivity 45%; lower finds more.
Balanced is the calibrated anchor — every per-category level is tuned and measured at that position — and the advanced slider runs 10% to 100% in steps of 5.
Always hide these takes a name plus either Exact text or Pattern (advanced), with a Case sensitive toggle, and redacts on top of whatever the detector finds.

Never hide these matches exactly on the normalised value (case, spaces and punctuation ignored), applies in every category and never expires; Always allow well-known companies covers 221 shipped names in the Company names category only.
The Overview tab shows the row 'Kinds of data we look for' as '{n} of 21' and warns in amber at zero: 'Protection is on, but nothing is ticked — so nothing will ever be found.'

Saving is one button, Save All Changes; success toasts 'Saved successfully!', while a rejected pattern still saves everything else and reports 'Saved, with notes' plus 'Saved, but N custom term(s) were rejected and are not in force.'

actionChecks.label: Add a company term and an exception
actionChecks.hint: Settings → Organisation → Privacy Shield → What we look for → Your own words and exceptions, then Save All Changes.

endpoints.returns: the saved shield config object for the learner’s own organisation (membership is enough to read it); customSensitiveTerms[] holds the Always hide these rows ({id,label,pattern,type,caseSensitive}) and piiAllowTerms[] the Never hide these values as plain strings

criteria.label: One term of your own is saved under Always hide these
criteria.hint: Add a row under Always hide these (name plus text or pattern) and press Save All Changes — a rejected pattern is not stored.
criteria.rule: GET the org shield config; customSensitiveTerms is a non-empty array (default config has none)

criteria.label: One exception is saved under Never hide these
criteria.hint: Add your organisation’s full name under Never hide these and press Save All Changes.
criteria.rule: GET the org shield config; piiAllowTerms is a non-empty array (defaults to [], and the built-in well-known-companies list is a separate flag)
